opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it comes down to a pretty simple belief: representation is the foundation of intelligence. Whatever a system ends up doing, whether it's recognizing objects, generating images, answering questions, or acting in the world, it first has to build some internal description of what it's seeing. If that description is good, a lot of downstream problems become easy. If it's bad, no amount of clever engineering on top really saves you.

When I started working on vision, the field was very task-driven. You had a dataset and a benchmark, and you designed a model to push the number up. That was useful, but I kept noticing that the real progress, the things that lasted, came from better representations. ResNet wasn't a classification trick; it was a way to learn deeper and richer features. Self-supervised learning was exciting because it suggested representations could come from the structure of the data itself rather than human labels. So I came to see representation learning as the thread connecting many things that look different on the surface.

There's also a more philosophical reason. Language models have shown how far you can go with a good representation of text, but text is a compressed, human-curated view of the world. The physical world is far richer, and vision is one of our main windows into it. I don't think we've figured out what the right visual representation is. We don't have the equivalent of next-token prediction that clearly works for vision. That's a big open problem, and I find it much more interesting than optimizing a specific application.

And I think representation learning connects to where the field is going. People talk about world models, embodied agents, multimodal systems. Underneath all of them is the same question: how do you learn an internal model of the world that is general, grounded, and useful for reasoning and acting? Generative models, diffusion models, and recognition models are all, in a sense, different angles on that question. Recently I've been interested in how generation and representation relate, for example whether good generative models actually need good representations, and whether you can bring them together more explicitly.

So it's less that I picked a topic and more that, every time I followed a problem down far enough, I ended up at the same place: what is the right representation? That question still feels unsolved, and I think it's one of the most important ones for getting to more general intelligence. That's why I want to keep working on it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the right representation remains an unsolved question and calls it an important reason to continue, but it does not identify many unresolved problems in representation learning; it frames the motivation mainly as one central open question.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a very simple belief: whatever the model ends up doing, whether it's generating images, understanding video, or reasoning in language, the thing underneath all of it is representation. If the internal representation is good, a lot of downstream problems become easy, almost trivial. If it's bad, you can pile on all the tricks you want and you're still fighting the model.

Looking back at my own path, that thread was there from the beginning even when I didn't name it that way. Working on ResNeXt, on ConvNeXt, on self-supervised methods like MoCo and MAE, on the surface those look like architecture projects or training-recipe projects. But the real question was always the same: how do we get a network to carry a representation of the world that is general, transferable, and honest about structure? Architecture is just one lever for that. Data is another. The objective is another.

The second reason is that I think representation learning is where the real scientific questions in deep learning live. Scaling works, everyone knows that now. But scaling tells you what happens when you push harder, not why. When I look at something like why diffusion models trained purely to denoise end up with surprisingly good internal features, or why aligning a generative model's hidden states with a strong visual encoder makes it train faster and generate better, those feel like genuine puzzles. They are not solved by more GPUs. They are solved by understanding what a representation is and what makes one better than another.

And honestly there is a personal element. The field moves fast and it's easy to chase whatever is hot each quarter. Having one question I keep coming back to gives me a way to decide what's worth doing. If a project teaches me something about representation, I'll do it even if it's unfashionable. If it doesn't, I'm probably not the right person for it. That constraint has been very freeing.

r001.rationale: He says representation learning is where deep learning’s real scientific questions remain, gives examples of genuine puzzles, and identifies that as a reason he keeps pursuing it.

astra-6.text:
For me, representation learning is a way of asking a very fundamental question: how do we turn raw observations into something a machine can use to understand the world? In vision, you start with pixels, but the things you care about—objects, relationships, actions—aren’t explicitly given to you. The model has to learn a useful structure from that input.

What keeps me interested is that this question persists even as the methods change. You can change the architecture, the training objective, or the source of supervision, but you’re still asking: what has the model learned to represent, and how useful is that representation when you move beyond the task it was trained on?

And that connects a lot of research directions that might otherwise look separate. Recognition, generation, learning across different modalities—all of them raise questions about what information a model captures and how it organizes that information. I like having that underlying question as a guide. It gives me room to explore new methods while still working toward a deeper understanding of how learning works.

r001.rationale: The response says representation learning raises a persistent fundamental question and connects research directions, but it does not identify many unresolved problems as Xie’s reason for pursuing it.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, representation learning is a way to connect a lot of the questions I care about. We observe the world through pixels, language, sound, and actions, but the raw data itself isn’t necessarily the right space for understanding or reasoning. The question is: what should a model extract from that data, and how can it learn to organize that information in a useful way?

What interests me is that this question stays relevant even as the methods change. You can change the architecture, the training objective, or the source of supervision, but you’re still asking what the model has learned about the world. Which distinctions does it preserve? What does it ignore? Can that knowledge transfer to a new task or a new environment?

So I see representation learning as a long-term research direction rather than a particular technique. It gives me a consistent question to pursue while leaving room to explore very different approaches. And it connects the practical goal of building better systems with the scientific goal of understanding why those systems work.

r001.rationale: The response says representation learning connects many questions and remains relevant across changing methods, but it does not identify many unresolved problems as Saining Xie’s reason for pursuing it.
